title: Historicals: All the Romans of SAGA
content:
With SAGA: Age of Caesars finally here, it's time to tackle the thorniest problem in buying and playing Roman miniatures: the bewildering diversity of Romes! We have, depending on your definition of Roman, five SAGA Ages where you can find a Roman Army list, and each one could (or should) have different miniatures associated with it. Luckily, if a miniatures manufacturer makes Historicals, it very very probably makes some Romans. Imperial, Republican, and Late Romans are massively popular ranges, so get out there and find the exact minis you want by trawling through all of our favourite sites. If you're diving into the classical world for the first time with Age of Caesars it can be a very confusing mix of loricas, legions and ages, so let's dive in and look at which miniatures match each battle board.

Age of Hannibal - Republican Romans

Most of us probably had our first encounter with Republican Roman armies through Rome: Total War, and, if you did, the cries of Hastati! Principes! Triarii! will be burned into your brain. From around 300BC to 100BC, the Roman army fought virtually everyone in the Mediterranean - Carthage, the Greek states, other Italians - until a slow organisational evolution transformed it into something much closer to what we usually think of as the Legion. This army was, to a great extent, stratified by social class, with three ranks of Legion infantry, wealthier cavalry and allied Infantry. Equipment and armour slowly changed throughout the period, with Greek-style Bronze Cuirasses and Italian short swords replaced by chainmail and the classic Gladius and Pilum over the 2nd century BC. Soldiers had to supply their own equipment though, so presumably this would have been fairly heterodox throughout!

Hastati, with a carthaginian head. From Republican Romans (1) Credit: Lenoon

Age of Hannibal features The Republic of Rome, a flexible board with a balance of offensive and defensive abilities with a strong focus on units of warriors. Your army must have more units of warriors on foot than levies, and more than twice the number of warriors on foot than hearthguard. Nicely, this sticks very close to the organisation of the Republican army, giving you a thematic and accurate-for-SAGA force.

Velites - Conscripts from the (near) poorest class of Romans, lightly and inexpensively armed. They were deployed as light infantry, and in SAGA terms will end up being your Javelin-equipped Levy.

Hastati - The younger conscripts, the Hastati (literally "spear bearers") were deployed at the front line of the legion. Armed with spears (later, pila), they would most likely have had a pectoral plate, helmet and shield as their major protection. These are your Warriors on Foot.

Principes - Slightly older (20s to 30s) conscripts, the Principes were the second line of the legion, most likely armed in a very similar way to the Hastati. These are more Warriors on Foot.

Triarii - The oldest cohort (30s to 40s), the Triarii were a heavy reserve force rather than the all-conquering spear gods they end up in the Total War series. These are your Hearthguard on Foot.

Equites - The cavalry of the Roman Republic was provided by those rich enough to support their own horse, forming the upper levels of the conscripted citizenry. They were paid more, treated better and died in occasionally society-destabilising numbers. They operated as heavy cavalry, with greek-style breastplates, small shields and spears or hefty two-handed lances. In Age of Hannibal, you can have one unit of Warriors on Horses.

Socii - The Socii were allied and tributary soldiers, called upon by the Republic to bolster the Roman line. When called from Italian states it's probable that they operated and were equipped much the same as the legion - but why not go a little further afield and use other classical age models with different kit? These would be a good place to represent Mercenary Units. 

Where to Buy Republican Romans

Lots of manufacturers make Republican Romans, due to the all-powerful allure of refighting the Punic Wars. The easiest place to go though, is Victrix, for the simple and convincing reason that you can pick up a single bag of miniatures and you're done. Victrix makes three Republican Infantry sets - Rome's Legions of the Republic 1, 2 and Allied Italian Legions. These are, more or less, the same set with different armour. All three allow you to make a rounded SAGA list for Age of Hannibal, with 36 Legionaries that can be Hastati or Principes (with 8 Triarii thrown in there too), 18 Velites and a smattering of command. The differences are in armour styles. If you want to model the First Punic War pick up Legions of the Republic 2 (pectoral armour), the second Punic War go for Legions 1 (chainmail), and if you'd like to look less strictly Roman and more like one of the other Italian city states, go for Allied Legions.

Victrix Republican Romans - Credit: Victrix

One bag will get you an entire SAGA army, but if you'd like to go further and bring along a few more options, Victrix also do Republican Cavalry which forms 1.5 points of Warriors.

Age of Caesars - Many Romes, One Emperor (Sometimes)

The Age of Caesars spans from slightly before there was a Caesar to around the 3rd century AD, and while the Roman army did vary and change significantly over the period, this is the classic, classical, image of the Roman Legion. Roman Citizens served as legionaries, eventually as a volunteer, professional army, with non-citizen soldiers serving as Auxilia and soldiers from outside the boundaries of the empire forming units of Numeri. Age of Caesars includes the Imperial Roman Army (around 30BC to somewhere in the 3-400s), the Caesarian/Late Republican Legions (slightly earlier) and the Palmyran Romans (270-273AD) Over the period, the equipment of Legionaries slowly changed, though reduced to 28mm scale these changes are mostly minor.

Romans! (credit: Ilor)

Legionaries - Organised into centuries (~80 fighting men) and cohorts (480), the Legionaries were heavily armed, very heavily armoured and fought predominantly as infantry. They were the hard core of the Roman army, and are represented by Legionaries in Age of Caesars.

Auxilia - Auxilia were non-citizen residents of the Roman empire, who could win citizenship by surviving a 25 year term (god knows what % of recruits managed that!). They provided archers, slingers, cavalry, javelinmen, elephants, and spearmen to the Army. They will be Warriors (No special equipment, mounted, ranged, and elephant) and occasionally Levy in Age of Caesars.

Numeri - Hired/pledged soldiers from beyond the empire, Numeri were armed with whatever their group usually had! This is a good opportunity to pick up some non-roman units for use as Mercenaries, Levy or Warriors. 

Where to Buy Caesarian Romans

This is where the armour nerdery kicks in! Late Republican and Caesar's legions (Julius connotation) were organised similarly to the Imperial Legions (Augustus onward connotation). The vast majority of Mini manufacturers use a shorthand visual difference: Chainmail vs Segmented armour.

Warlord Caesarian Romans

Chainmail, the Lorica hamata, was increasingly common in Roman armies throughout the Second Century BC, becoming standard equipment by around 120BC. It is used all the way through the Imperial Roman period, so picking up chainmail-armoured legionaries will do you from 100BC to 300AD, if you can ignore that most Caesarian Romans have Coolus helmets (you can). Warlord Games have a nice box of Legionaries in lorica hamata with Julius Caesar era helmets which will make you exactly 4 points of Legionaries. For Ranged or Mounted Warriors and Levy, head back to Victrix, who have an excellent range of Auxilia in Cavalry, Archer and Infantry forms. If you want to pick up some metals to go along with these, Wargames Foundry have a fantastically characterful range where you can pick up some incredibly grizzled Centurions.

Where to Buy Imperial Romans

The classic legionary image, the Imperial Romans represent the height of the Pax Romana, the period of Roman-enforced economic and cultural hegemony over the European and North African world. In real life it was likely equipment was never quite as homogenous as on the table, but why not lean into it! The lorica segmentata, the banded/segmented armour that endures as the most famous image of the Roman legionary, is introduced some time around the BC/AD border, and becomes at least fairly widespread quite quickly. Accompanying it is the Imperial Helmet, oblong scutum (shield) and heavy pilum, making for an Asterix-style image of Roman equipment perfection!

Hell yeah, Victrix Romans (credit: Ilor)

Imperial Romans are available virtually everywhere miniatures are sold, but again, if you want that single bag draw, Victrix' new Imperial Roman Warband gets you a full 6 point army as long as you want all-Legionaries and a ballista! Otherwise, Victrix Early Imperial Roman Legionaries (Advancing/Attacking) each get you 4 points of Legionaries, which can be easily supported via Auxilia for ranged or mounted Warriors and Levies.

Where to Buy Palmyran Romans

The Palmyrans provide a slightly different take on Roman equipment, with the short lived indepedent Palmyran Empire arising out of a slow disintegration of centralised control over the empire during the 3rd Century. They're styled in SAGA as a blend of Eastern and Roman battle boards, which likely goes at least some way to representing the complex blend of identities that emerged, and supported independence, out on the Eastern fringe of the Empire. While Palmyra didn't last very long, there's a surprising amount of miniatures available. While the kitbasher might want to pick up some Imperial Roman kits alongside Persian or Sassanid plastics, you probably want to go with Armorum and Aquila Miniatures who have a solid range, while Essex Miniatures have a good range of Persians and Romans to mix and match from - though beware these are 25mm rather than 28.

Age of Invasions - Romans

Age of Invasions picks up story with the Romans in SAGA, with a focus on the late 3rd to 5th century AD. Age of Invasions portrays the Roman Empire at bay, holding on where it can as the systems underpinning the western half of the empire begin to fall apart. This happened in different places at different times, Age of Invasions slightly squashes this together into a single battle board with a strong focus on momentum through the Impetus ability. It's a very defensive board that rewards planning and organisation, which is why I can't get my head around it at all.

The late Roman army was split into smaller, more flexible, units, with the Legions - once mighty if cumbersome behemoths - brought into line with the smaller Auxilia legions. Over the period Age of Invasions depicts, the idea of the "Border Force", the Limitanei, became more prominent, with garrisons holding down an increasingly tenuous border. Equipment differentiation begins to grade into each other and Roman armies become less standardised and more influenced by their local area. Trousers replace tunics and kilts, especially on colder borders, hamata returns to replace the segmentata and older helmet styles are replaced by ridge, nasal and cavalry helmets. The armies become increasingly regional and complex, but can be very roughly classed into:

Comitatenses and Limitanei - The inheritors of the Legionary heavy infantry, who fought with darts, sword and typically oval shield. Comitatenses refers to soldiers of the mobile armies (as contrasted to the Limitanei, the garrison forces), who were possibly a bit better equipped, armed and trained, used as a trouble shooting (literally) force when customs disputes, raids and migrations overwhelmed the Limtanei. Ranging from Heavy Infantry to medium, ranged or non ranged, These are your Warriors, Warriors with Bows and potentially Levy.

Equites - The Late Roman period saw a resurgence of Heavy Cavalry, back to prominence after the Legionary core of the Imperial period was seen to be too slow to react to the various border threats. These could vary from Legionary-style cavalry all the way up to Cataphracts, incredibly heavily armoured cavalrymen clad head to hoof in mail. In Age of Invasions, these form your Hearthguard on Horse and Hearthguard Cataphracts

Foederati - Troops recruited from treaty-bound nations and tribes around the edges of the Empire. Goths, Saxons, Franks and the like could all go from sometime mercenaries to treaty partners to enemies fluidly! Foederati (which doesn't mean Foe as in enemy, interestingly), were often groups of "barbarian" mercenaries with whatever equipment the Romans could hire at the time. These could be all sorts of units in SAGA terms, from just about anywhere in the late Roman world - Hearthguard could make your army represent one of the "Barbarian" Emperors, Warriors could be a mix of elite soldiers and foreign specialists, levy would show a mass conscription to meet a crisis and mercenaries can add some unusual rules and models to an otherwise standard force.

Where to Buy Late Romans

Armoured Goth warriors, who will also look good as late romans. Credit: Lupe

Another area where everyone makes models, Late Romans have the huge advantage of being fairly heterogenous in terms of kit and equipment, so mixing ranges has a huge pull. Victrix have a lovely late Roman set that will do you well but I am a relentless kitbasher so my eye is drawn to the Wargames Atlantic Decline and Fall range. There's quite a few kits here - two types of Roman armour, Goths, an army builder set we reviewed positively, and light cavalry. The exciting bit is that all of these come with the same arm, waist and head joints, so you can buy a ton of different kits, chop all the bits off the sprue and kitbash anything you like, from very regular Romans to foederati armed with whatever's left in the bargain bin of the Constantinople storehouses. Great fun!

Age of Vikings - Last Romans

After 300 years of slowly, and then quickly, falling apart, the Romans of Age of Invasions, battered and bloody, crop up again as the Last Romans in Age of Vikings. This is a good bit of confusing naming, because by some accounts they're not "Roman" - Rome is ruled by someone very very different at this point - and they're certainly not the last. The Last Romans is a combined arms board in an era of charging at the enemy waving a sword about, using heavy shooting power and reserve forces of hearthguard and warriors to kill whatever makes it through. Your warriors, hearthguard and levy all have access to ranged weapons, so you can shoot, feint and strategise your way through the barbarians beyond the Theodosian walls.

Byzantine cavalry. So hot right now. Credit - Rick H

The Byzantine army went through almost as many rejigs as the Classical Roman one did, but from this point on the Legions are long gone, and the core unit of organisation is much more feudal - the Theme. Themes (Themata) were regional centres with associated armies, largely concentrated in Anatolia as the last true bastion of Eastern Roman power that could plausibly withstand something like "a load of people turn up and start burning things down". The standing army, as opposed to whatever guys the Empire could hire, was organised in the Tagmata system, slightly smaller and weaker individually than the legions. The age of Vikings board represents an Eastern Empire forced onto the defensive, carving up territory into more easily defended subdivisions, waiting for the last ride of the Emperors across the Balkans (spoiler for Age of Crusades there!). Your armies will be made of:

Tagmata Soldiers - Your Hearthguard, mounted on horses and blending centuries of lessons learned from Cataphracts and Eastern horsemen, these are very clearly a transition between the heavily armed shock cavalry of the late empire and the mail armoured proto-knight we know from Norman and Carolingian sources. Last Roman hearthguard can hit like a brick, but there's always very few of them!

Welcome also to the hearthguard club the Varangian Guard! Finally, the Eastern Empire gets in on the big hairy guys with big axes trend with the traveling mercenary/bodyguards/kingmakers/Western Europeans of the Varangians. Armed with Heavy weapons, they form a hard hitting deterrent for anyone trying to charge your archers.

Theme Soldiers - These are your bog-standard warriors, who may or may not be professional fighters. They're armed with spears, shields, darts and lamellar armour, looking very much like a continuation of the Late Roman soldier, or bows. These form your warriors.

Psiloi - Light skirmishers, retaining all the low status and basic equipment of their ancestors. These add, in sufficient numbers, serious short and medium ranged firepower to the Last Romans, in addition to being generally annoying and skirmishing out front. These are your levy.

Where to Buy Last Romans

Byzantine Mounted Archers from Footsore.

These Last Romans can still be represented with Late Roman troops so everything above applies. If you want to stick to plastic, mix up Late Roman and Byzantine (see below) plastics to add some heterodox themes. Otherwise, you’re looking for Early Byzantine miniatures, or suitably rough looking Byzantines. Footsore, Gripping Beast and Aventine all have large ranges.

Age of Crusades - Byzantines

A Byzantine army is a formidable sight. Credit - Rick H, London SAGA Mead Hall

The Byzantine army age of crusades lets you take your Eastern Romans right up to the bitter end, with a board that brings elements of Invasions and Vikings with it. You’ll need to plan ahead with Domestikos, rely on close cooperation between units and try to keep your warriors alive with stacks of defence dice as long as possible. All the while you want to be harassing, moving and firing and generally annoying the slower latins and avoiding the faster Islamic armies. To pull that off, you have the 11th century Byzantine army to help you:

Hearthguard - Mounted lancers that might look suspiciously like Normans or Anglo Danes on Balkan horses, because they absolutely were! Mixed in there will be retainers and Eastern Empire equipped knight-equivalents, but a man in mail on a horse can be from anywhere! Varangians still hang around, and receive a massive influx of Anglo Dane nobility after 1066.

Warriors - Again, mostly mounted (probably more in the game than in life!), these are the final evolution of late Roman cavalry, merged with the tactics and experiences of fighting Islamic armies on the Anatolian border.

Levy - Still Psiloi, these are the farmers, smallholders, townsmen and occasional professional foot soldiers that your Doux has levied from his immediate area.

There’s still a lot of evolution to go even in this late period. After taking a massive battering at the battle of mamzikert, the Eastern Roman Empire has its (almost) last hurrah just before the Crusades. The reforms of the Kommennos killed off the last lingering remnants of the themes and legions, replacing them with something that for our purposes looks much like the medieval armies of a century or two later: professional soldiers, feudal retainers and specialist mercenaries. The redesigned Byzantine Army manages to take back a bit of the old imperial stomping ground of the Balkans, and even calls in the wild and uncouth successors to the western empire for a bit of religious warfare the emperor is absolutely sure he can control. I’m not sure it was quite as all mounted as the SAGA board make out, but lighter troops and mounted archers were definitely a key part of the army. While it’s on the way out, the Empire still manages another three hundred and a bit years in one form or another, but here we have the last gasp of the SAGA Romans.

Where to Buy Byzantines

You might not need many, but it's always good to have some spearmen. Byzantine Spearmen from Fireforge Miniatures.

Byzantines have a bewildering amount of representation in metal miniatures, but for plastics go with Fireforge. Some of the sculpts might be a little chunky, but there's a very solid range here of infantry, light and heavy cavalry and - for now - they're the only people in the market!

If you want to go down the Byzantine armies as a collection of troops on retainer, you can go to Victrix for Norman and Islamic Infantry - mixing up the sets will make for some great Anatolian troops  Armenians, and Constantinople-based Normans.

Oops! Too Many Romes

Of course, this is history - and more than that, it's Roman history - so nothing is ever that simple. There are far, far more Romes than that. On a very generous basis you can make a claim for a whole lot more, so in the interests of completeness here's a very, very brief line on just some of the major contenders for, "Oh man there's too many Romes":

Age of Invasions - Goths

Are the Romans the people who rule Rome, the leaders educated by Rome or the people who claim to be the Roman Emperors? Whatever the case, Theodoric and the Ostrogoths have a solid claim to it. Ruling over Italy - and claiming the Imperial title - from 493 to 526, Theoderic recieved the previously defunct vestments of the Western Imperial throne from the Eastern Emperor, making the Ostrogoths another Roman board in all but name. This board is all combat all the time, representing a wave of experienced troops crashing into already exhausted enemies.

Age of Vikings - Carolingians

Another hairy guy who technically kind of ruled a version of the Roman Empire, Charlemagne and the Carolingians certainly told everyone they were the inheritors of the Roman Empire, helped by the fact dodgy Pope Leo III crowned him as Emperor in 800AD. The Carolingian board is all about organisation, striking at weak points and overwhelming in detail. The key ability Proelium acts a little like Late Roman impetus, a nice thematic link to the inheritance Charlemagne claimed.

Age of Chivalry - Papacy

If the Roman Emperor lives in Rome, is richer than God and runs a world spanning empire from an Italian throne, then the papacy is surely the western Roman Empire by any other name? The Papal States turn up in Age of Chivalry as a variant for the Condotierri board, where the unique quirk is a lot of shooting and the ability to reroll SAGA dice en masse.

Age of Chivalry - Germany

is the Roman Empire whatever people say is the Roman Empire? I’m not going to make the classic joke but if so, the Germans of the age of Chivalry are the latest - and last -  Rome in SAGA. The German board inherits elements of the Gothic one in Invasions - tire your enemy out, manage your own fatigue and finally win the argument of what’s Roman, Holy and an Empire when everyone else is too tired to carry on!

No, No More Romes

It's really quite fantastic that SAGA lets you play Rome all the way from the Punic War to the 4th Crusade, with boards that work to at least the vague feel and theme of what was happening in the Empire at the time. There are - of course - many more SAGA boards that could claim to be Roman, without even touching on the Sultanate of Rum, Romania, the mess that is Britain and a succession of new-Romes (nationalist connotation). But, with a Rome for nearly every age, the gauntlet is down - who among you can fight to become the ultimate Augustus from 300Bc to 1450AD, and keep the flame of the Romanitas burning on the SAGA tables?

If you'd like to pick up Wargames Atlantic kits and support Tabletop Battles while you're at it, get them through our affiliate link. You can also support Tabletop Battles by buying sweet, sweet Victrix kits through our affiliate link. title: MTG Arena codes for August 2026
content:
MTG Arena codes are an essential, mostly free kick-start for your digital collection, unlocking new Magic: The Gathering cards, booster packs, XP, and cosmetic items like card sleeves, avatars, and more. Read on to find all working MTGA codes in 2026, as well as full instructions on how to redeem promo codes on PC and mobile.

Each month, as the MTG release schedule rolls on, we trawl Wizards' announcements about new MTG sets to update this list, telling you which codes currently work; which have expired; and which brand-new codes have sprung up for the game. The good news is that you can still unlock free cards to boost your MTG Arena decks.

Here's how to get MTGA codes:

  • All free MTG Arena codes in August 2026
  • Unlock the cabbage companion
  • MTG Arena rewards
  • How to redeem MTG Arena codes
  • Where to find more MTGA codes
  • All expired MTGA codes

All free MTG Arena codes in August 2026

For the first time in ages, and lasting until August 27, there actually are MTG Arena codes to be used! A chain of riddles, released alongside the Hobbit set, will win you some cards, card styles and a unique avatar. Here's what to do:

Right now, if you check your inbox, you'll find a riddle. Input the answer as an MTG Arena code in the store to unlock a reward and the next riddle. Keep going until you've answered all eight, then create a deck with all eight of the cards you just unlocked. 

It doesn't have to be legal, or even have the correct number of cards, so just plonk them all in and save it. Name the deck 'Riddles in the Dark', and you'll receive a Bilbo avatar.

If you want to try to solve the riddles yourself, exit this page right now. We're assuming you're here for the answers, which you'll find below.

  • Riddle #1: Mountain (The Mountain-king's Return card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #2: Teeth (Gnashing of Teeth card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #3: Wind (Velvetwing Butterflies card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #4: Darkness (Gathering of Darkness card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #5: Egg (Well-Worn Spatula card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #6: Fish (Lake-town Mariners card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #7: Time (Stone by Sunlight card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #8: Precious (My Precious rare card and borderless card style)

In case you skimmed the bit above, you now need to make a deck called Riddles in the Dark with all eight of these cards to unlock the final reward.

Unlock the cabbage companion

Would you like to have a high fidelity cabbage for your companion? Of course you would! This nutritious friend is available as a free easter egg, added to celebrate the MTG Avatar: The Last Airbender set in 2025. You can unlock it by playing any matched game on the Avatar battlefield, and clicking on the Cabbage Merchant's cart until it explodes. Do this and you'll be rewarded with your very own cabbage.

Can't find the cart? It's at the top of the battlefield, just to the left of your opponent's profile picture.

Is the cabbage companion better than the beachball or the pet rock? That's for you to judge.

MTG Arena rewards

These days, Wizards hands out free booster packs as MTG Arena rewards to celebrate the release of new sets. These arrive directly in your in-game inbox without the need to redeem a code. Plus, new players who complete the how to play tutorial are greeted with a whole stack of reward packs to crack open from the last couple of years' worth of sets (plus a selection of variant land cards to use).

Here are all the rewards each MTG Arena player has access to, as of August 2026:

  • 3 x Alchemy: Strixhaven boosters
  • 3 x Secrets of Strixhaven boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Lorwyn boosters
  • 3 x Lorwyn: Eclipsed boosters
  • 3 x Avatar: The Last Airbender boosters
  • 3 x Through the Omenpaths boosters
  • 3 x Edge of Eternities boosters
  • 3 x Magic: The Gathering - Final Fantasy boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Tarkir boosters
  • 3 x Tarkir: Dragonstorm boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Aetherdrift boosters
  • 3 x Aetherdrift boosters
  • 3 x MTG Foundations boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Duskmourn boosters
  • 3 x Duskmourn boosters
  • 3 x Bloomburrow boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Bloomburrow boosters
  • 3 x Modern Horizons 3 boosters
  • 3 x Lost Caverns of Ixalan boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Ixalan boosters
  • 3 x Murders at Karlov Manor boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Karlov Manor boosters
  • 3 x Shadows Over Innistrad Remastered boosters
  • 3 x Phyrexia: All Will Be One boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Phyrexia boosters
  • 3 x Outlaws of Thunder Junction boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Thunder Junction boosters
  • 3 x The Lord of the Rings: Tales of Middle-earth boosters
  • 3 x Wilds of Eldraine boosters
  • 3 x Alchemy: Eldraine boosters
  • 3 x Khans of Tarkir boosters
  • 3 x March of the Machine boosters
  • 3 x March of the Machine: The Aftermath boosters
  • 1 x Basic Wastes Land (from Explorer Anthology 2)
  • 6 x Alchemy: Brothers War boosters

How to redeem MTG Arena codes

There are two ways to redeem MTG Arena codes on PC, and both are dead easy - just pick your method below and follow our step-by-step guide.

How to redeem codes in the Arena client

The most common and simplest way to cash in your codes is directly inside the MTG Arena client. Here's how to do it:

1. Open up the game on PC and click on the 'Store' tab at the top of the page.

2. You'll see a small oval text box in the top right corner, with 'Redeem Code' written inside (we've highlighted it in red in the picture above).

3. Copy your code into the box and hit enter.

4. Your reward automatically appears in your account!

How to redeem codes via your Wizards account

If you'd rather not boot up the game, you can also redeem codes by entering them into your Wizards of the Coast account page. Here's how you do this:

1. Log in using your MTG Arena details, and on the right-hand side of your account dashboard, you'll find a nice, big 'Redeem a code' box.

2. Paste the code inside and click 'Redeem'.

3. The goods will appear in your account next time you log in to the Arena game client.

How to redeem MTGA codes on mobile

If you're primarily a mobile MTGA player and want to redeem codes on your phone, the process can feel a bit more convoluted, because - frustratingly - there's still no way to redeem codes directly through the iOS and Android versions of the game.

The main way to get the job done is simply via mobile web, with the following steps:

  1. Log in to your Wizards account via your mobile browser.
  2. Scroll down to the 'Redeem a Code' box as shown in the image above.
  3. Enter your code, and click 'Redeem'.
  4. Your rewards will show up next time you log into the game.

If everything's worked correctly, you'll see a little green message pop up that reads "Code redeemed successfully", as seen above.

However, if you really want to make things difficult for yourself, you can access that same account-based process from within the MTG Arena mobile client. We don't recommend it, though, because it's janky as all hell - it's far easier just to hop over to your mobile browser and do it there.

Where to find more MTGA codes

If you've already used all the free codes available, and still want to expand your collection of planeswalkers, creatures, and fancy land cosmetics, there are a few other places where you can sometimes get your hands on more MTGA codes to redeem. You can do this either by buying select Magic products that include Arena freebies, or else staying alert for new promo codes and other fans' unused codes shared online.

The main options to try are:

  • Physical Magic: The Gathering products
  • Social media giveaways and competitions
  • Promo codes from local game stores
  • MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

Physical Magic: The Gathering products

Unlike the Pokémon TCG, not every sealed pack of Magic cards comes with a digital unlock code included - but some physical MTG products do give you a code into the bargain, to grow your digital collection as well as your cardboard mountain. There are three types of products you can buy for this.

Prerelease kits

Wizards of the Coast launches each new Magic: The Gathering set with a pre-release event focused on in-person games in local game stores, selling Prerelease kits of six brand new boosters.

Since 2025, these prerelease kits have no longer included MTG Arena codes packed in the box. Instead, you'll register your Arena account when you attend the pre-release event at a physical store, and your free boosters will appear in your account when you next log in.

However, older prerelease kits can still be found for sale which do contain Arena codes. If you buy one of the following recent Prerelease kits, you can use the included code to unlock MTG Arena boosters for the corresponding set:

Product Reward Approx. Price Link
Murders at Karlov Manor Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon
Lost Caverns of Ixalan Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon
Outlaws of Thunder Junction Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters  $30 Buy at Amazon 
Commander Legends: Battle for Baldur's Gate Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $47 Buy at Amazon
Kaldheim Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $32 Buy at Amazon
Ikoria Prerelease kit 6 Arena boosters $56 Buy at Amazon
Zendikar Rising Prelease kit 6 Arena boosters $27 Buy at Amazon

Starter kits

Starter kits are designed to get newbies into Magic: The Gathering, so they offer up two pre-constructed decks. The kits also come with a code that unlocks each deck in MTG Arena, too.

Buying a second-hand starter kit might mean that your code has already been used, but if you can get one new (or from a reputable, code-selling source), these are the decks to look out for:

  • Bloomburrow Starter Kit
  • Wilds of Eldraine Starter Kit
  • Lord of the Rings Starter Kit
  • Starter Kit 2023
  • Starter Kit 2022
  • Starter Kit 2021
  • Core Set Starter Kit 2021

Planeswalker decks

All physical Planeswalker decks released between the October 2018 set Guilds of Ravnica and Core Set 2021 came with a one-time code to unlock their cards in MTG Arena, so you could use all the same cards online.

Sadly, the older codes from these decks have now expired, and the decks themselves are very difficult to come by (they're all unavailable on Amazon US and UK) - so you'll struggle to find an unopened copy with an intact code for a reasonable price. Even more sadly, free codes isn't a trend that was carried on by the far more available Commander precons.

If you really want the physical cards too, though, it might be worth the hunt; here's the full list of decks with (we think) still functioning codes:

  • Ashiok, Shaper of Fears
  • Basri, Devoted Paladin
  • Chandra, Flame's Catalyst
  • Elspeth, Undaunted Hero
  • Liliana, Death Mage
  • Oko, The Trickster Planeswalker
  • Rowan, Fearless Sparkmage
  • Teferi, Timeless Voyager
  • Vivien's Hunt (released in a Hot Pocket promo)

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes are found in Wizards of the Coast's limited edition, premium Secret Lair boxed sets of one-off collectible cards. The rewards vary, but usually, they unlock exclusive cards and cosmetics.

You can get some pretty sweet, limited edition skins, though - for example, if you bought the 'Warhammer Bundle' during the October 2023 Warhammer 40k Secret Lair, you got two codes, each good for ten premium card sleeves showing the 40k-ified versions of classic cards:

  • Merciless Executioner as "Ork Kommando"
  • Aggravated Assault
  • Krenko, Tin Street Kingpin as "Makari the Lucky Grot"
  • Zurgo Helmsmasher as "Ghazghkull, Prophet of the Waaagh!"
  • Blind Obedience
  • Danitha Capashen, Paragon as "Neave Blacktalon"
  • Najeela, the Blade-Blossom as "Archaeon the Everchosen"
  • Scourge of the Throne as "Stardrake"

Beware, though - this is often the priciest way to find new codes. Each Secret Lair 'drop' can cost anything from $20 to several hundred bucks. We only recommend going this way if you really want the physical cards your codes will come bundled with.

Social media giveaways and competitions

If you're a social media-savvy Magic fan, another way to nab a cheeky extra code is through giveaways or competitions run by major MTG content creators, influencers, or simply kind-hearted fans sharing codes they don't need or want for themselves.

MTGA Codes, a retail website that collects unwanted and unused Arena codes and sells them directly online, regularly runs such giveaways to drive engagement on its Twitter account (@MTGA_CODES).

There's no way to know when such giveaways will take place, or exactly who's going to be doing them - but we can recommend a few creators you should follow just for regular, great content and commentary on Magic and Arena, who have been known to give away MTGA codes in the past:

This isn't a regular occurrence, though, and it's entirely dependent on Wizards' ongoing strategy for working with game stores - if you're angling for extra codes, we'd recommend checking in with the staff at your LGS to see if there's anything on offer.

In the past, Wizards of the Coast has collaborated with other big brands to offer MTG Arena promo codes as a bonus for their subscribers - and, back in 2019, it gave away free unlock codes as a benefit for the Twitch Prime service (now merged with Amazon Prime Gaming).

All you had to do to get the code was sign into your Twitch Prime account, check the 'Loot' section, click on 'claim', and it would generate a code for you to redeem directly in the Arena client.

Sadly, we haven't seen any more new MTGA codes come through this service in the years since - but there's always a chance, so if you're constantly on the hunt for fresh codes, it's worth periodically checking in on your Prime Gaming account (there's also a bunch of free videogame downloads and other goodies there, of course).

How to play Truth or Dare

      2. Sit in a rough circle - so everyone knows whose turn is next.
      3. Start playing - each player, in turn, gets asked: Truth or Dare?
        1. If they pick Truth, either the group as a whole, or the player who went last, asks them one of our questions above, and they must answer honestly, or perform a forfeit.
        2. If they pick Dare, it's the same - but they must perform a Dare, or face a forfeit if they refuse to try.
      4. Play as long as everyone's having fun - there's no scoring or winning in Truth or dare; the game just keeps going until most players want to stop (maybe you're getting bored, or it's time to head to the club). The key thing is to wrap things up before anyone stops having fun.

Top tips for a successful Truth or Dare night

We're a bit old and boring these days, but we played more than our share of Truth or Dare in college, and as seasoned game analyzers, we've got some useful tips you should follow to have the best possible game:

      • Read the room - Truth or Dare is a game about making each other a bit uncomfortable, that's the fun of it - but there's a fine line between breaking down barriers with your friends, and making people mad, sad, or freaked out. Especially if you're the party host, be mindful of how good a time everyone's having, and wade in politely if you think it's necessary to keep the whole group having fun.
      • Consider the couples - Couples are great for Truths, as they know where all each other's bodies are buried, and can unearth the most entertaining stuff. But they can make things boring when it comes to spicy dares - where's the fun in forcing people to kiss someone that's already their partner? Consider using house rules to make sure couples don't lean on each other to avoid their duty to the game!
      • Set no-go areas if necessary - A game where everyone's expected to spill their deepest secrets, even embarrassing ones, can occasionally touch on topics or areas that are particularly sensitive for certain players, or could even bring up traumatic memories. As the host, if you're already aware of risks like that, think of a way to introduce a house rule that avoids it coming up, without 'outing' the person - there's no shame in having a banned topics list. It might sound over-cautious, but we've had some rough moments like this in the past, and everyone's there to have fun - so think about it.

That's all for now! If you made it through my juiciest Truth or Dare questions, you might also enjoy our world-leading guide to the best sex board games.

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! Dark Angels Dilemma, Giving Up the Game, and Pod Problems
content:
Welcome back once again to Mayday, Miss Marcy!, in which I take your reader submitted queries and provide them with the advice vested in me by being alive for a while. You'd think there'd be a better pedigree, but sometimes that's all it takes! If you've never read this column before, we take 3 questions sent in by readers from various places and try to come up with actual (and sometimes entertaining!) answers to them! If you'd like to know how to get your own questions submitted to the column, please read the instructions below!

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

ALSO, we're heading OUT of Summer, so if you have some Back to School, Fall, or similar turn of the seasons questions, let us hear it!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

Last week, Condit joined me to help out, and we had a great comment from Mintopo that I wanted to give a shout out to in regards to the question "The Girl Reading This"; I really agree with the comment and think its great advice! As always, I love getting your questions but also your comments. Now on to this week's questions!

Greg, Line 1, Greg,

Dear Miss Marcy,
As a young collector of Dark Angels i have been having trouble deciding what to add to my collection. I have the Marine half of Armageddon the new combat patrol and the lion as well as a few other kitbashes / cheap ebay finds. I'm not asking for a shopping list but just a way to decide what should be a priority and what I can wait to get.
From a Totally non traitorous Dark Angel
Dear Totally Non Traitorous,
I may be stepping into the domain of Greg here for a moment, but Dark Angels do rule severly hard, and I applaud your choice of Chapter. I assume you are maybe looking to potentially play in 30k and 40k, as you mention The Lion, so you might be on the right path for collecting your army by looking second-hand due to the differences in units between the 2 games. 40k is going to be a lot easier to shop for in general, since you'll be looking to field mostly Primaris Marines and Terminators, all of which are easily available from Games Workshop themselves and without a lot of extra work involved. 30k you might be best suited going the secondhand market, as the older scale models are going to be available in bulk. From there, you'll need to find heraldry and other options to help you do kitbashes, and making a full army is really just going to come down to settling on what units you want and then tracking them down. If I could make some suggestions, aside from heroic units like Lazarus, Belial, Asmodai, Azrael and an Interrogator Chaplain, you will probably also want to look into bikes!
If you want to provide us with more detailed questions, such as what type of game you'll be playing more often, we will happily provide you with answers from our vast array of Dark Angels specialists!
Edit: Thanks to GW's website being very, uh, good at being a website, it did not include The Lion in the 40k section under "Dark Angels" when I looked. The advice is still generally the same.

They Return

Dear Miss Marcy,
I am more of a tabletop hoarder than a gamer unfortunately. I have yet again lost interest in some games I worked on hobbying (building, magnetizing bases, priming, basing), and am not thinking about trading the projects in. This time however the issue is not one that has come up before. In the past it was due to me thinking the game was awesome, but no one played in my area. This time however it is because I really do not gel with a majority of the players in my area. The thought of playing with some of the folks (they could be described as "those guys") makes me not want to engage with the game anymore. Them being smaller games in my area they are going to be my main opponent. In your opinion what should I do? I already have decided to go with the most played games in my area because I do enjoy the hobby, games, and a huge bulk of the player base. Any advice is appreciated.
- The Insulin Dependent "Wargamer"
Dear Insulin Dependent,
Nice to hear from you again! For those who haven't been reading the column for a long time, Insulin is one of our longtime writers, and it's always a pleasure to hear from you. Sorry to hear that the smaller game you've found here is unfortunately mired in "Those Guys" sorts of players, because I absolutely have been there before. even longer time readers may know that my favorite miniature game of all time was Guild Ball, and when that game died I tried to find many other games to fit the same feeling, which never, sadly, materialized for me. Part of that is that the groups I tried to meet with and play with often were filled with "Those Guys" who tended to trade chudd-y jokes, present an unsportsmanlike and unfriendly atmosphere, and often just tended to repel me from the games I wanted to try playing.
The sad truth to this situation is that you should consider either shelving that game for now or offloading it if you need the space and clarity in your life. It sucks to say that your best option is to sell out of the game, but if the only people who are going to play it are people you would rather not socialize with or be associated with, then you are going to really struggle to ever actually play the game. It will also just sit there and remind you of the fact that you've had this problem, and make you unhappy looking at it; I won't name the games themselves on my end, but let's just say that I sold myself out of about 4 games for this very reason over a number of years, and while it made me sad that I never got to experience the games fully, I also realized I would have been miserable and not wanted to play anyway.

Pod Bound

Dear Marcy,

I've been playing with a Magic Pod for a while now, and while it seemed like the dream, it has sort of become very stale. Our Pod does not really like to invest in change in new cards, decks, or anything, and after a while it has become difficult to constantly play against the same decks over and over again. The worse problem is that I do actually like to invest and try new things, which has also gotten some annoying comments from my pod about "upsetting" the balance of things.

I love playing Magic and my Pod is my primary way of doing so, and without them I very likely won't have much option or ability to play the game at all. That being said, it feels like my interest in the game is being drawn away from me anyway, because I would rather just not play than face the same exact decks every week. Considering the decks are 100 cards, it feels like I know what every player is going to play by heart now.
Unenchanted Magic

Dear Unenchanted,

Ah, Magic Pods. They are actually a lifeline to a lot of players, because they provide stability and often a very consistent schedule of players who do not always have the time or interest in more competitive formats like Standard or Modern at the competitive level. They come with the caveat/problem that you've mentioned, though, which is that they can get stale VERY fast if the players are committed to their "routine". I think the best way you can perhaps approach this if you feel like you'd like them to change is try to sell them on some form of group investment or concepts that can help shake things up. I think there's about a 50/50 chance that this doesn't work, though, because sometimes groups of people just want to get together and play the same game over and over again not because of the challenge or the struggle, but mostly because of the socialization and regularity aspect of it.

If your group declines and you're feeling that frustrated, though, I think there is some self-defeat built in to "I won't get to play". You already said that you are not having fun playing, and almost would prefer not to play if you're just doing the same thing over and over again, so what really changes if you stopped going? You also could absolutely find a new pod I am pretty sure, but it would just require putting yourself out there. And that can be just as challenging or difficult as other parts, but do consider that you're opting to sit around doing something you don't enjoy, OR finding a new group or way to spend your free time. Unless this Pod is consisting of your closest friends and loved ones, separating yourself from them might hurt at first, but I think it will be better than being miserable, which you clearly are.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: This high octane Warmachine lore bundle packs in 41 fantasy books for $30
content:
UK-based tabletop games maker Steamforged Games has partnered up with Humble Bundle for a new bundle deal, packed with Warmachine tie-in novels and short story anthologies. There's 41 books in total, ranging from the backstories for iconic Warcaster characters like Lieutenant Caine and Captain Phinneus Shae, to major moments in the metaplot like the second Cygnaran civil war and the return of the Dragonfather Toruk to the main continent of Immoren.

If you got into Warmachine for the first time after Steamforged Games acquired it in 2024, you might only be aware of the lore inside the Warmachine app. But from the release of the very first edition in 2003, the game had a moving metaplot that was expanded with supplement books, short stories in No Quarter magazine, and eventually a range of novels under the Skull Island Expeditions imprint.

I read a bunch of those books back in the day - they were always good pulpy fun, even if they weren't all high art. Dan Wells' 'The Butcher of Khardov' stands out in my memory as being really good, giving a believable and tragic backstory to Orsus Zoktavir; a real feat of storytelling, given that any other time he appears in a story, he's a barely coherent homicidal maniac.

Obviously, this bundle will appeal most to people who are already familiar with the Iron Kingdoms setting, but if you enjoy action-packed fantasy stories I recommend you look into the setting a little before passing it over. The Iron Kingdoms might appear to be just another Eberron-adjacent 'magic plus technology' setting, but while that's definitely part of the story, it also puts some really interesting spins on classic tropes.

The setting has deep metaphysics, and the relationship between magic, the gods, the creation of the world, and what happens to souls before life and after death is all really interesting. That leads into interesting some very deep, slow-burn plotlines; there are long term threads involving a cult of science-magicians who worship a constellation and are trying to re-align the planetary leylines in sympathy with it, and an entire empire of pirates and necromancers ruled by a dragon, just to pick out a few highlights.

Getting the 41 eBooks and digital anthologies in this bundle will cost you $30 (£22.23). It's available on Humble Bundle until Wednesday September 9.

You can also go double or quits and pay £60 (£44.46) to get not one, but two entire TTRPGs. The two versions of the Iron Kingdoms RPG are completely different, one using an adapted version of the Warmachine miniature wargame rules (a genuinely great system, but definitely better if you use miniatures and battlemaps), the other based on DnD 5th edition. Pledging at this level unlocks 65 items split between the two games, from core rules and major supplements through to maps and adventures.

Has a range of tie-in novels ever left an impression on you, or greatly exceeded your estimations for licensed fiction? I will go to bat for the Horus Heresy books, despite the low points the series sometimes slumps to, because the best stories are genuinely peerless. If you know of a range of tie-in books that's way better than it has any right to be, the Wargamer Discord community would love to hear your recommendations.

title: Pokémon Pocket reveals Team Rocket set with EVIL legendary birds
content:
Prepare for trouble! Pokémon Pocket is releasing a Team Rocket set next week, on August 27, 2026, and it just dropped a trailer showing off loads of the new cards. No doubt DeNA is hoping this set, Rocket's Ambition, will be just as much of a draw as the TCG's Destined Rivals.

Judging by the tone of the trailer, Rocket's Ambition portrays the Rocket Gang as more mischievous than downright dastardly, and most of the cards seem more silly and fun than powerful and competitive.

I'm talking about cards like Team Rocket's Thieving Machine, which nicks a random item from your opponent's Discard pile. Team Rocket's Master Plan confuses your opponent's Pokémon, but has a 50/50 chance to also confuse your own.

Team Rocket's Boss (not sure why they didn't just write Giovanni) lets you force your opponent to play their basic Pokémon, which might be useful for Team Rocket's Zapdos, which can hit the bench. More importantly, it could be great in a Suicune ex deck.

Team Rocket's Articuno damages your own bench, meanwhile which seems rough right now, but will be great if Pocket ever gets a Munkidori equivalent.

Team Rocket's Moltres is a little different, however. It's looking a lot like Charizard. While its ability is less consistent, it is a basic Pokémon, so you don't need to devote nearly as many slots in your deck to supporting it.

All in all, the cards shown off so far seem fairly weak - nothing stands out as immediately exciting. However, we know better than to judge a release off just a handful of cards, and even if it's not a total powerhouse set, we can already see there's some great art.

That trailer has me pretty pumped in fact. It might be time for me to re-download Pocket.

title: Cronch Does the Hobby Challenge at the Warhammer Newport Open 2026
content:
At Tabletop Battles, we sometimes receive products or event invites from Warhammer for review. For this event, though, Rich purchased his own ticket, and attendance was not based on any existing relationship with, or an invite from, Games Workshop.

Although Britain is undeniably the home of Warhammer, and we’re lucky enough to have Warhammer World on our (figurative) doorsteps, for a while now we’ve lacked large Warhammer-run con-style events similar to things like the Tacoma Open in the USA. 2026 has seen that change, and the Newport Open is the second of the American-style Open events that Warhammer have run in the UK. Unlike the earlier Birmingham Open, though, which piggybacked off the UK Games Expo, Newport is an entirely Warhammer offering. It was my first time at an Open, and I was keen to see what it had to offer.

I’d originally planned to enter the three-day, eight-game Age of Sigmar GT, but I’m out of practice and have been riding a wave of burnout, and ultimately decided that it might be a bit much to jump into without planning and practice. I ended up refunding my ticket and pondering over what to do instead. Having been asking for this style of event in every possible survey opportunity for the last few years, I felt like it would have been a cop-out not to attend and support it, so I settled on the Hobby Challenge activity. Low pressure, and low commitment; something where I wouldn’t be inconveniencing anybody if I decided to hit the bricks and go home early.

“But Cronch, what’s the Hobby Challenge?” I hear you ask. Understandable, given that at least some of the event pages ahead of the event have listed “Hobby Challenge” with no further elaboration.

What Is the Hobby Challenge?

The Hobby Challenge has appeared at various Warhammer Opens in the past, and is a weekend-long kitbashing and painting challenge. The easiest visual representation is probably the episodes of Scrap Demon on Warhammer TV, and the Hobby Challenge takes that idea and extends it from a short video to a weekend-long activity. A ticket for the challenge (£50 at Newport, bookable in advance or pay on the day) gets you a boxed centrepiece model, an oval or rectangular base, unlimited access to the big pile of sprues, use of tools, brushes, paints, and the ubiquitous Warhammer Open swag box, with the end goal of creating a diorama or conversion to share with your peers.

The team running the challenge set a theme for each event - at Newport, this revolved around the idea of a space hulk crashing on Armageddon, with both Imperial and Ork forces dispatched into the wreck to retrieve something precious. The theme informs both the initial models available to choose from and at least some of the sprues available in the sprue pile, with Newport attendees able to choose from a selection of Ork and Marine characters.

Newport Open 2026's Hobby Challenge story. Credit: Rich Nutter

From there, it’s a simple enough prospect. Build your model, converting if you wish, and use the sprue pile to build a scene, or perhaps a big conversion like a vehicle, sticking to the suggested theme as much or as little as you like. When you’re ready, the event team will prime your mini in a colour of your choice (including zenithals if you like), and then you can use the paints and brushes supplied to paint up your creation. At the end of the weekend, there’s some judging for awards around theme, painting, converting, and an overall winner is chosen. Anything you’ve created is yours to keep.

Does that sound like fun? It is!

Friday: The Build

I had an unhurried start to my Open weekend, arriving at the International Convention Centre Wales at around 2pm. Checking in was easy, and I was surprised to receive the 2026 swag box with my entry. This contained a decent selection of merch items: a lanyard, a battle journal notebook with pen, some 40mm casino chip-style objective markers, a metal die, some 40k and AoS-themed sticker sheets, and a £10 voucher for the event store (off a minimum £25 purchase). Nothing mind-blowingly important or valuable, but a nice add-on when the ticket was only £50, compared to £125 for the GTs.

Swag box contents. Credit: Rich Nutter

More importantly, the box contained two items that would help with the hobby challenge. First up, an A4 cutting mat, replete with a Warlord Titan design. This is cool as hell, and will definitely get some use at home. Secondly, there was a foam insert with slots for a water pot, paints, and brushes, the idea being that you could use the swag box as a kind of project box for the weekend. This was a thoughtful addition that I got plenty of use out of during the event, even when just trying to keep my paints organised on the desk.

Swag box in hand, I headed through to the main hall, taking in the scale of the event before heading to the Hobby Challenge area. I was greeted by the team running the event, who explained this event’s lore: a Space Hulk crashes into Armageddon, and Imperial and Ork forces both dispatch forces inside to retrieve something. They then offered me a choice of my centrepiece model and a base to build around. The options were:

  • Beastboss
  • Warboss in Mega Armour
  • Boss Snikrot
  • Phobos Librarian
  • Lieutenant in Reiver Armour
  • Maybe one more Space Marine that I can’t remember!

I have a Marine army, so I opted to go against my usual instincts and pick an Ork. In the end, I opted for the Warboss in Mega Armour, a model I’ve admired from afar since it came out, but never bought. I also selected a large oval base, before immediately realising that that would be hard to make straight lines on, and swapping it for a large rectangle instead. Even now, a plan was forming.

I’d decided that, sprues willing, I’d like to make some kind of Space Hulk corridor, or hatchway, with the Warboss facing off against an as-yet undetermined opponent. The rectangular base would describe the rough size of my diorama, and I’d need to source parts to make a main corridor wall along the long edge, a floor, potentially an end wall and/or hatch, some ideally Imperial opponents, and some battlefield scatter. Having found a place to sit and deposit my stuff, it was time to brave The Sprue Pile.

The sprue pile was, frankly, magnificent.

The sprue pile. Credit: Rich Nutter

I’m not sure what I was expecting, but there was a lot of stuff here. Most, if not all, sprues were incomplete or broken down in some way, but there was a healthy mix of terrain, Ork, and Imperial parts, plus the occasional bit of something more esoteric, like Liberators from Age of Sigmar. To add some excitement, staff would occasionally announce the addition of something new to the pile, usually with a narrative reason. As an example, at one point we got a couple of lines of narrative about ancient warriors in relic marks of armour emerging from the warp to join the fray, which heralded the addition of some Horus Heresy kits to the pile.

First forays. Credit: Rich Nutter'

Initially I grabbed a few sprues that stood out to me - some barricades from the updated Aegis Defence Line, some stockade walls from the Battlezone: Fronteris range, a couple of random vents that I couldn’t identify, and a sprue of Death Korps of Krieg infantry that I thought might serve as my Imperial forces. With a bit of experimentation, I realised that I could cut the spikes off of the stockade walls, invert one, and pin/glue them together to make a wall that seemed about the right size for the interior of a Space Hulk corridor. Conveniently, it was also very close to the length of the base I’d chosen!

Taking shape. Credit: Rich Nutter

I’d identified that the aegis barricades might look good butted up against each other as either a vertically or horizontally opening door, but that meant I would need to build an end wall for them to mount to. Salvation came in the form of the top panel from a Rhino, trimmed flat to give a hatch hole that my blast doors would cover well. Some cutting and glueing of some wall corner pieces later, and I had the bones of my idea together. I also found a couple of broken-up floor tiles (possibly from a Necromunda kit?), which I glued down both to get the height of the doors right, and to square up the angle between the walls. In hindsight, this was an error, as I couldn’t find any more of these tiles later!

With the glue setting, I opted to head outside for some food, look around the game hall and store, say hi to Corrode playing in the 40k GT, and generally kill time for a little while. Refreshed, I came back to my table and decided to build my Warboss. I did consider a conversion, and hunted for a head in the sprue pile to give him a gas mask or similar (I was imagining the heads from the Heresy Ogryns), but I couldn’t find anything, and decided to build him as-is. Luckily for me, in the intervening time somebody had returned a load of flat panels to the sprue table, and I was able to grab a couple of octagonal plates from the Aegis Line to fill out my floor needs, as well as some corrugated pieces that I cut down to fill in the windows on the wall, and some assorted small parts to fill in gaps in the Rhino wall.

Further progress. Credit: Rich Nutter

This left me with some strange-shaped gaps in my floor, until a bolt of inspiration hit. I’d already planned to really rust this corridor up, and I’d also generated a sizable amount of plastic shrapnel during my construction attempts. I filled my gaps with glue, sprinkled on a bunch of plastic rubble, and then dripped more glue on. I also found some Astrogranite on the painting table, which I thinned and stippled around the scenery, ready to look like patches of rust texture after priming. Finally, I found bits to make three Imperials - an Arbitrator (with a stern-looking Sororitas head), a Cadian, and a Krieg trooper. I wasn’t sure if I’d use them all, but it was good to have them built at least.

Deciding that it was time to paint, but also that my work needed more time for glue and texture to dry, I opted to call it a day at around 7 PM and head to my hotel for check-in before finding a local pub for dinner. I was pretty pleased with what I’d managed to build in a day, and was looking forward to getting the paints out after a good night’s sleep.

End of day 1, ready to prime. Credit: Rich Nutter

I do think it’s worth mentioning here that alongside the clippers, mould line scraper, plastic glue, paints and brushes provided by the event, I brought some of my own equipment from home, mainly my building toolkit (reliable clippers, scalpel, files/sandpaper, hobby drill, plastic and super glue, small clamps), and around 20 reliable paints/washes alongside a wet palette, my brushes, and some corks/wire for subassemblies. I wasn’t really sure whether this was encouraged or not, and couldn’t find anything about it in the rules, so I ended up asking a friend who had done it before, and they informed me that I’d be fine. I was far from the only person with my own stuff, and it seemed like the staff were happy for people to use the tools that they were comfortable with. Obviously, Warhammer aren’t going to supply drills and knives at an event that kids can (and do) enter!

Saturday: Painting

Refreshed, showered, and breakfasted, I made my way back to the hall at around 10 AM on Saturday. First things first, my now dry piece would need priming. Staff were taking care of this, with a range of neutral colours available - they also seemed open to the idea of doing a layered zenithal for people hoping to take advantage of some built-in shading. I asked for my main built to be primed black, and gave them the Ork on one painting handle and the three Imperials pinned to another, all to be done in grey. They were sorted in record time, and I could get down to business.

Slop it up. Credit: Rich Nutter

I tackled the corridor first, as I knew it would take a while. Straight over the black, I slopped on big, thinned-down patches of Warhammer Colour Mournfang Brown, Skrag Brown and Balor Brown, then left these to dry for an hour or two. Once dry, I added some Troll Slayer Orange in more targeted spots, and then once this was dry I drybrushed the whole thing softly with Leadbelcher, trying to build up the metal tone gradually and not erase the brown tones. This is a great method taught to me by a friend who is a terrain painting whiz, and it came in clutch here for getting a lot of colour down quickly. With that done, the terrain is basically done for now, barring some details later.

Ork skin done. Credit: Rich Nutter

In the gaps between terrain steps, I tackled the Warboss. I used Pro Acryl Bright Green as a base, shaded by mixing in some Pro Acryl Dark Hot Pink and layered with Bright Yellow Green. At this point, I was very glad to have put the Rogue Hobbies Pro Acryl signature set in my case, as well as the Pro Acryl Bright Yellow Green (an all-time favourite). I really wanted to paint the Boss’ armour red, maybe with yellow details, but decided that compositionally it would not stand out from the rusty background well, so ultimately I chose blue instead. This was based with Warhammer Colour Kantor Blue, before being layered and highlighted with more of the Pro Acryl set. From there, I filled in metals and details with a bunch of colours, and then moved on to the Cadian.

Ork done, also featuring drybrushed metals on the diorama base. Credit: Rich Nutter

I’m not going to teach you how to suck eggs (paint Guardsmen), but I will highlight one notable point when I realised I absolutely did not have the right colour for the Cadian’s classic green armour. The event organisers had provided a lot of paint, but not covering every colour in the range. Fortunately, after some hunting (and briefly considering buying a paint from the store), I found a single pot of Contrast Creed Camo buried behind about 15 pots of Bad Moon Yellow, and the day was saved. Over the rest of the day I finished the Cadian, painted the crates I’d added to the corridor, and basecoated the Arbitrator's armour, alongside wandering around the event checking out the tables, admiring the pre-painted terrain (very nice), catching up with some of my Age of Sigmar club, and generally soaking up the atmosphere.

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

After round 6 of the GT was finished, I met up with Corrode for a late-night katsu curry delivered to a dark picnic bench outside the ICC before returning to the hotel for more sleep.

Rich's final Hobby Challenge entry with minis in place. Credit: Rich Nutter

Sunday: More Painting, and Results

I overslept a little on Sunday, and after breakfast and checking out of the hotel, it was nearly 11 AM before I made it back to the hobby area. Fortunately, I had a pretty defined set of goals for the day: finish the Arbitrator, and paint the Krieg soldier. I started with the Arbitrator, and the high proportion of black armour meant it was fairly swift going. I highlighted it up with blue-black colours, sticking to greys on the black leather areas to differentiate them. The hair was basecoated Warhammer Colour Corax White, then washed a couple of times with Russ Grey thinned with Lahmian Medium before being highlighted with a pure white.

The swag box did indeed come in useful. Credit: Rich Nutter

Whilst finishing the Arbitrator, I noticed a couple of places where I’d failed to add pouches/holsters, and there were obvious gaps. I opted to fill these in with pouches and grenades from a Cadian sprue, which I superglued on and then painted over bare plastic. At the same time, I managed to find a voxcaster backpack for the Krieg soldier, replacing the non-standard bag I’d added in place of a correct piece the day before.

With a couple of hours left, it was time to get the Krieg guardsman done. Fortunately, this wasn’t my first rodeo in this regard, and I got it done to a decent standard in the time available. With about 30 minutes left, my friend Chris came over and helpfully pointed at my diorama and said something along the lines of “it would look better with some hazard stripes” which felt a bit like being hit with a hammer. I decided to rush and try it, and managed to cover up my pretty messy stripes with rust and weathering to give a serviceable effect.

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

Last-minute hazard stripes, and the base is complete. Credit: Rich Nutter

With the clock ticking down (we had until 3 PM to finish), I blacked out the edges of the diorama, glued and pinned the minis in place, and then took it across to the display table to put it alongside everyone else’s creations. I’m so happy with what I produced! I had an idea and executed on it. I’m really pleased with the level of finish I achieved in a weekend.

Rich's final Hobby Challenge entry with minis in place. Credit: Rich Nutter

It was really amazing to see what everyone had come up with, spanning smaller dioramas like mine all the way up to huge, bulky Ork Gargants. I had a great time chatting to people about what we’d made, and if I have one regret for the event, it’s that I mostly kept to myself while working rather than making more of an effort to chat to my fellow Hobby Challengers across the weekend!

A selection of other entries. Credit: Rich Nutter

Amazing Ork Gargant which won Best Conversion. Credit: Rich Nutter

I liked this layout. Credit: Rich Nutter

Another take on the classic Space Hulk encounter. Credit: Rich Nutter

After we’d all had a chance to look around, we were ushered away so that the judges could review the entries and decide on the winners. After 45 minutes or so of waiting with bated breath, we were called back. Prizes were given out for best theme, best conversion, best painted, and a youngbloods prize for under 16s. Then it was time to announce the overall winner, and…

The Hobby Challenge Trophy. Credit: Rich Nutter

I won! Unbelievable! I really wasn’t expecting to, given the quality of the other offerings, but the judges said they liked the combination of painting and conversion execution whilst also sticking closely to the narrative theme of the event. My prize: the Hobby Challenge trophy, lovingly built and sprayed by the event staff while we were working on our entries. I was excitedly informed that it features 240 skulls and 15 grots - can you spot them all?

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

Alongside the trophy, I was also given a Horus Heresy boxed set and the promise of a Spearhead or Combat Patrol of my choice. I’m really impressed with this level of prize support, and grateful to win!

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

Armageddon Space Hulk diorama. Credit: Rich Nutter

Wrapping Up

So, all in all, I had a great time doing the Hobby Challenge at the Newport Open! Obviously I’m thrilled to have won, but even putting that aside, I had a great time just sitting and hobbying towards a defined goal, rummaging through sprues, and soaking up the atmosphere of the expo. Unlike tournaments, which often leave me feeling drained, I came home feeling refreshed and reinvigorated. The venue was also great, with helpful, friendly staff, great air conditioning, decent enough food options, and ample (if slightly expensive) parking. If you’d like to attend an Open but don’t want to play games, then I’d thoroughly recommend the Hobby Challenge as a fun and engaging option that’s good value for money. Do let us know if you attend one, or have done so in the past, and share your creations!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.

title: Leaked Secret Lair MTG deck is stuffed with staples and $300+ in card value
content:
The full decklist for an upcoming Secret Lair Commander deck has been shared online, and if these leaks are accurate, this MTG deck is stuffed with powerful and desirable staples. The Odds and Ends deck is led by Yennett, Cryptic Sovereign, so it's all about cheating out powerful cards with odd mana costs. It features artwork by Ricardo Cavalo, who has produced several Secret Lair cards and whose work has a colorful cartoonist vibe. Also, it's always covered in eyeballs.

Leaks surrounding this deck have been circulating online for months, so we've already seen some images of the cards - in fact, we knew about its existence in late 2025. But now, the entire decklist has emerged in a Discord and been quickly recreated on the deckbuilding site Moxfield. And while the deck itself doesn't feel very tightly constructed, with some rather random inclusions, fans are very excited by the sheer number of busted and expensive cards in here.

Pride of place, there's Esper Sentinel, a Commander staple that has gradually risen to $60 over the years because it's one of the most efficient and effective card draw spells available in its color, and Wizards stubbornly refuses to reprint it.

There's also a Sensei's Divining Top, a top-deck control card that provides surprising utility and fuels dangerous combos - and that you'd struggle to buy for less than $50.

Though it's a far cheaper card than these two, fans also seem super excited about the land card, Yavimaya Cradle of Growth, which lets all lands count as forests. I suppose no one likes spending $15 on a land, so getting it bundled here is a big plus.

While these are the highlights, there are no shortage of powerful, costly creatures in the list, like Toxril and Void Winnower, as well as a couple more great mana rocks and lands like Command Beacon and Misleading Signpost. There are lots and lots of cards at the $15-20 mark.

There's also some downright odd inclusions. For instance, Space Beleren, widely considered a troll card for the constant book-keeping it requires, tracking the 'sector' of every single creature. Then there's Time Stop, an expensive spell which ends the turn. It doesn't have an odd mana cost even, not that you'd want to cheat it out on your turn if it did.

Plenty of fans are bound to buy Odds and End even if they have no intention of playing it out the box, just to break it down for parts. There's no confirmation of what this deck will be retailing for, but these Secret Lair precons normally sell for $150. Depending on which outlets you look at, there's between $300 and $450 of card value in total here, making this a bargain offer.

I actually am wondering if this deck will be popular enough to bring down the value of cards like Esper Sentinel, and make them that little bit more reachable for the rest of us.

That will largely depend on whether Wizards tries out its new strategy and makes it print-to-demand for the first day. It implemented this for the Hatsune Miku deck and as a direct response to the backlash to Goblin Storm. Here's the relevant portion of the relevant article:

"This sale is an experiment with introducing a 24-hour limited order window on products meant to be playable out of the box. So, this could include things like Commander decks, specialty products like the Secret Lair Dandân Deck, or anything else wild we think of down the line that may have the unique combination of high demand and out-of-the-box playability."

That certainly suggests that the upcoming Odds and Ends deck would be included in the experiment too, but it's far from a guarantee or a promise.

Are you picking this one up? Share your opinion in the Wargamer Discord.
